title: From Shadow Agents to Employee Agents: how we build autonomous agents at Rappi
summary: Decisions, mistakes, and lessons from building AgentOS, the platform where more than 600 agents live today
body_markdown:
# From Shadow Agents to Employee Agents: how we build autonomous agents at Rappi


## Decisions, mistakes, and lessons from building AgentOS, the platform where more than 600 agents live today


[Jonatan Ponzo](https://medium.com/@ponzo.jonatan?source=post_page---byline--644244ff4c3a-----------------------------------------)


17 min read


·


4 days ago


--


Every day, before the team starts working, one of our project manager agents at Rappi reviews what happened in its project’s repositories, which releases went to prod, what was said in yesterday’s meetings, and updates the status of every task so it reflects what actually happened — not what someone remembered to write down. Then it publishes the report on Slack. It never forgets, it doesn’t take vacations, and it doesn’t mind doing it. It has its own Slack user, its own calendar, and its own credentials in our project management platform. It doesn’t belong to anyone in particular: it belongs to the team.


It’s not the only one. Another agent staffs an internal support channel and resolves eight out of ten questions without escalating to a human. Others diagnose operational issues across orders, stores, and couriers. Others pick up the tasks that project manager left planned and turn them into pull requests ready for review. Many of them were created by people who a year ago didn’t know what a system prompt was. And some of our main user-facing agents — the ones that talk to real users over the web and WhatsApp — live on the same platform.


Three months after launching AgentOS — eighteen since we started experimenting with our first agents — we have over 600 agents and 130 agencies for internal use running in production, 20 thousand conversations in the last 30 days, and 165 people who created or edited one in that same month.


We didn’t get there in one leap. We started with what we call Shadow Agents — assistants that act as a shadow of the person using them — and ended up with Employee Agents: agents that work as one more member of the team. Between one and the other there are several layers, and we discovered each one by hitting the limits of the previous one. This article is that journey: what the agent was missing at each stage, what we built to cover it, and what we got wrong along the way. It’s not absolute truth — it’s how we did it.


## Adapting to a landscape that changes every day


In early 2025, with MCP freshly released, we started experimenting with our first AI agent: a dish-and-restaurant recommender that ended up becoming the AI assistant in the Rappi app. We learned about models, sessions, prompts, skills, tools, guardrails, memory, tracing, and much more. But the lesson that weighed the most was a different one: in this ecosystem, everything changes too fast. New models every month, frameworks born and dead within a quarter, protocols evolving week by week.


The answer was a design decision that ran through everything that came after: abstract ourselves from providers and frameworks, and stick to open protocols (mainly MCP and A2A). Concretely: we implemented a model proxy with a standard interface, automatic tracing, and an MCP Gateway. We centralized usage, budget, and security controls for the whole company. And all of it available self-service from DevEx, our developer portal, so our engineering teams could build their agents or publish their own MCP servers in a standardized, self-service way.


## From chat to the first agents


While we were upgrading our platform for the engineering team, something was happening in the rest of the company: people in business and operations areas were moving from simple chats to building their own agents in Claude Code or ChatGPT. They were useful to whoever created them but hard to share. The result was predictable: dozens of similar agents — inefficient, wildly uneven in quality, and disconnected from Rappi’s ecosystem. Everyone reinvented the wheel, and the knowledge stayed trapped in individual sessions.


That’s where AgentOS was born: a platform to create and manage agents with no code and no deep AI knowledge. But the vision from day one was not “an internal ChatGPT” — it was considerably more ambitious: 100% autonomous agents with their own identity. Not assistants that augment a human, but agents that work like one more employee.


That vision set three rules:


- **No-code.** It has to be possible to create an agent without developing or deploying code. If creating an agent requires an engineer, the platform serves only a fraction of the company.
- **Remote runtime.** The agent runs on our infrastructure, not on anyone’s machine, and can therefore work while its user is offline.
- **Real autonomy.** The agent has to be able to work without anyone invoking it, and belong to a team rather than a person: it can’t die because its creator went on vacation — or left the company.


## Build vs Buy


That vision also forced us to re-examine a reflex. As a platform team, our first question when facing a new project had always been what was available on the market to save us the cost of building and maintaining it. Over 2026 that equation changed a lot: the cost of implementation and maintenance depreciated drastically, and the flexibility of building something that fits exactly what you need started to weigh more. When we began designing AgentOS we evaluated the market options and none covered the three premises at once: no-code, remote runtime, and real autonomy. So we built it.


## Shadow Agents


We started with what we knew: Shadow Agents — agents that act under the identity of the user they’re talking to, with basic connectors (Slack, Gmail, Drive, Calendar, Snowflake). The name says it all: they are a shadow of the person, with nothing of their own. They can even write on Slack, but they do it under their creator’s borrowed identity, as if it were that person speaking. Even so, what used to be a prompt on someone’s machine became a team asset, and that alone was already an improvement.

Users quickly asked for more than reading emails and calendars: they wanted to operate on the business. We connected AgentOS to our MCP tools gateway (by then the technology team had already published several MCP servers on it) and agents could now act on orders, stores, couriers, and partners. That was the moment the platform stopped being a productivity assistant and became an operational tool.

## Agencies


With the platform up and running, use cases kept growing in complexity, and sometimes a single agent with skills wasn’t enough: the problem needed to be split. So we added agencies: several agents with specific roles working toward a common goal, like a team.


The first complex agency was Talk2Data, for building reports conversationally from the data in our warehouse: one agent understands the question, analyzes our data catalog and translates it into queries, another processes the results, another assembles the report. In a company with Rappi’s data volume and complexity, that process is anything but trivial, and it was the first sign that the unit of work wasn’t always going to be an agent — sometimes it would be a team of agents.


Today, almost one out of every four creations on the platform is an agency rather than a standalone agent.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


*AgentOS Agencies Catalog*


## From reactive to proactive


Up to this point, all our agents had something in common: they were reactive. However capable they were, alone or in an agency, they waited for someone to write to them. An employee doesn’t work that way: a good part of a team member’s value is in what they do without being asked.


We built scheduled tasks: internal periodic loops that let an agent wake up and act without anyone invoking it. Adoption was immediate, especially for daily business reports: agents that every morning query the warehouse, assemble their report, and publish it before the day starts.


And it was precisely that adoption that exposed the next gap — the most important of all.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


*AgentOS Scheduled Tasks*


## Real autonomy


An agent that runs every night and stops because its creator’s token expired is not autonomous. It’s a cron job with good manners.


The clearest case was Snowflake. For security reasons its credentials expire quickly, and daily business reports broke easily: the agent did its job until, one morning, it simply couldn’t query the warehouse. The same happened with Google Drive when an agent had to write a document, or with Slack when it had to publish a report. Shadow Agents acted with borrowed credentials, and borrowed credentials expire.


To be truly autonomous they needed credentials of their own: their own Google Workspace account, their own documents, their own queries against Snowflake, their own GitHub user, their own permissions in DevEx and in Atlas, our internal spec-driven project management platform. We progressively enabled an agent credentials mode in every connector, alongside the end-user credentials mode.


This was the turning point. An agent with its own identity stops being an extension of a person and becomes an actor in its own right within the organization. The project manager from the opening exists thanks to this layer. Its own GitHub, Atlas, and Calendar credentials are what let it work without depending on anyone being online: it reads the meetings, reviews the repos, and updates the tasks signing with its own name, not someone else’s.


And here comes the question anyone asks at this point: how do you control an agent like that? Our answer was to treat it, as much as possible, like one more member of the team.


- Agents belong to teams, not people, and their permissions are limited to that team’s resources (often, to a subset).
- Everything they do is traceable. There is no agent action without a record of who, what, how and when.
- On critical connectors, scope is limited by design. An agent can create pull requests, but not merge them. It can deploy to development, but not to production. It can edit a document only if its owner explicitly authorized it.
- Responsibility lies with the team that created it. If the agent makes a mistake, the responsibility is the team’s — same as with any new hire.


## Agents that evolve


With identity and credentials solved, the platform grew fast. Three capabilities finished shaping what we mean by “employee.”


## Sandbox


An agent could write code and had nowhere to test it: it delivered code no one had ever run, and it failed in CI. The same happened on the data side: agents brought back results from the warehouse and couldn’t process them.


So we gave every agent the option of having a sandbox using OpenSandbox: its own isolated execution environment where it can run code and work with files.


## It can learn


Our support agents investigated the same question three times. Someone asked something on Slack, the agent went to the code, found the answer, and explained it well; the next week, with someone else asking the same thing, it started over from scratch. They knew how to search, but had nowhere to leave what they had learned.


We gave them two distinct things. Memory, for what they need to remember about each user or entity they work with: the *who* . And an LLM Wiki, following Andrej Karpathy’s concept: a knowledge repository the agent itself writes and organizes at its own discretion — the *what it knows* .os


Press enter or click to view image in full size


*LLM Wikis built and maintained 100% by the agents*


Those support agents started with GitHub access and an empty wiki. Today they resolve ~80% of the questions they receive on Slack without escalating to a human, using knowledge they built themselves.


## It can be evaluated


An agent can start answering worse without anyone noticing. It doesn’t crash or throw errors: it just answers less and less well, and the team finds out when someone complains.

For that we built an evals service that evaluates agents’ real sessions using different types of judges and, in addition, allows simulating conversations with simulator agents before exposing them to users.

## Techie Efficiency decisions


Two decisions from this stage pursued the same thing: efficiency, both in context window usage and in infrastructure.


The first: the sandbox integrates natively with every connector. When it’s enabled, any connector can read its input from a file in the sandbox and write its output to another, instead of loading everything into the agent’s context. The agent works with the data as files — chaining the output of one connector into the input of the next — and only brings into its context what it actually needs. That saves context window (that is, cost, time, and quality) and saved us from building and maintaining a per-connector integration: any new connector added to the platform works with the sandbox without a single additional line of code.


The second: the sandbox is the only infrastructure an agent owns, and only when its owner decides it needs one. Because an agent is not a server: it’s a record in a database. When no one is talking to it, it consumes no resources. When a message arrives or a scheduled task fires, a pool of completely stateless runners receives what it needs to start the agentic loop (the agent’s configuration and the session id), and any node in the pool can serve any agent. With hundreds of agents running, they cost almost nothing while idle; scaling horizontally means adding runners.


Both are the same philosophy — one applied to context, the other to infrastructure: don’t pay for what you’re not using.


## Live Artifacts


A parallel problem had been growing with adoption: a lot of people used agents (or Claude/ChatGPT directly) to generate reports or UX prototypes, and those had no clear place to live. They ended up shared as loose HTML files on Slack: no access control, no stable URL, and outdated the day after they were generated.


For that we created Live Artifacts: sites published by agents, accessible to the rest of the company via a URL, with access controlled by their owner. A report stops being a file that ages in a folder and becomes a living page the agent keeps up to date; if it’s a daily report, the same URL always shows today’s version.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


Live Artifact built by an Operational Data Analyst Agent.


## Blending the agents into the organization


We had built agents that were, functionally, one more member of the team. And they lived in a tool you had to deliberately go into. You message the rest of Rappi’s employees on Slack; these you had to go find.


So we took them to where the people are. First, **Slack** : each agent with its own user, which anyone can message like a colleague, and which can also write proactively with its own identity — not a borrowed one. Second, **A2A** , the agent-to-agent communication protocol: agents can be integrated from outside the platform, and that’s how they started showing up as embedded copilots in the internal tools teams already use every day.


Taking agents to Slack had an additional effect on adoption: with them there, one message away, more people understood their potential and wanted to create their own. Today many of Rappi’s internal agents are built and operated by people without a strong technology background — from operations, business, or finance — who a year ago didn’t know what a system prompt was.


And the movement wasn’t only inward. Some of our main user-facing agents — exposed in our apps, on the web, and even through WhatsApp — also live on AgentOS.


## Agentic roles


With the platform’s core consolidated, the focus shifted to composing roles within the company, combining the capabilities as building blocks. Two cases show better than any other how far the pattern reaches: the project manager from the opening, and the development agency that works from what it plans.


## The project manager


Anyone who has managed a project knows the dilemma. A board that reflects the real state of the project costs hours: follow-up meetings to find out what happened, and then more time to pour it into tasks. And if nobody pays that cost, the board lies: it shows what someone remembered to update, not what happened.


It’s the kind of role we wouldn’t have imagined “automating” until recently, and it turned out to be one of the most natural for an Employee Agent. The morning we described in the first line of this article, reread through the platform’s eyes, is every layer working at once: a scheduled task wakes it up without anyone messaging it; its own credentials open GitHub, the deploys, the calendar, and Atlas; in its LLM Wiki it writes down the lessons relevant to its daily work; and its Slack user publishes the report, where anyone can reply, ask for detail, or correct it.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


AgentOS Product Manager Agent daily report


There’s a part we didn’t tell at the beginning: it also feeds the backlog. And it doesn’t do it by reading channels, but by asking a colleague. It consults AgentOS Coach, the platform’s support agent, about recurring errors, problems, or feature requests, and turns the answers into new tasks in Atlas. An agent interviewing another agent to plan the team’s work.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


*AgentOS Product Manager’s feeding the backlog*


It doesn’t make product decisions. It does what a good PM would love to delegate: making the board tell the truth. And unlike a GitHub–Jira integration, it understands context: it knows the PR merged yesterday closes the task discussed in Monday’s meeting, even if nobody linked the two.


## The development agency


On the other side of the board is the agency that executes. It’s an end-to-end agency made up of several agents with specific roles: planner, implementer, reviewer, tester, and QA. It takes the tasks the project manager created in Atlas, plans them, implements them, tests them, deploys to our development environment with its own credentials, and does QA, both local and remote (with Playwright for frontends). The result is a pull request with all the evidence of the process and a Slack message asking the team members for review.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


AgentOS Software Factory agency working in a task


Today, more than 60% of the PRs merged to ship features or fix bugs in AgentOS are made by this agency — created inside AgentOS itself. The team that maintains AgentOS is 2 people, who develop the big features or the ones involving important decisions, and who also review, approve, and deploy to production. The groundwork is done by the agency.


We started with AgentOS, but other Rappi teams are already adopting it progressively, starting with simple tasks and bugs and ramping up the complexity little by little.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


AgentOS Software Factory on Slack


## Same ingredients, other roles


**Operations** (business MCP tools + Slack). Diagnosis and management agents that operate on orders, stores, couriers, and partners. They’re the ones that turned the platform into an operational tool.


**Data analysis** (Snowflake + sandbox). Agencies like Talk2Data, which translate a natural-language question into queries against the warehouse, process the results, and build reports that used to require an analyst.


**User-facing support** (WhatsApp via A2A + agencies + Rappi MCP tools). Agents that talk to real Rappi users, on the same runtime, the same credentials, and the same evals as everyone else.


**Internal support** (GitHub + wiki + Slack + Rappi MCP tools). Several internal Slack support channels are staffed in the first instance by AgentOS agents. What they don’t know, they investigate and document in their wikis; what exceeds them, they escalate to the team via Slack. Like anyone new to the role.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


AgentOS Coach, the AgentOS Support agent in Slack


**SRE** (Slack + GitHub + sandbox + DevEx). It reviews alerts from unstable services, does the troubleshooting with its DevEx tools, and proposes a solution: a PR, a resource adjustment. The alerts still come in for now; the difference is that they arrive accompanied by a diagnosis and a proposal ready to validate.


An SRE Agent reviews autonomously detects and troubleshoots unstable services and proposes a fix


**UX prototypers** (sandbox + Live Artifacts). They turn ideas into navigable prototypes anyone in the company can try.


Each role is a different combination of the same ingredients: identity, credentials, connectors, sandbox, memory, evals, and a channel where the rest of the team already is.


## What we got wrong


We launched a platform that let you build agents in a thousand different ways, with control over the tiniest parameter. That unleashes enormous potential, but only if two things come with it — and we brought neither.


The first is a UX that supports both extremes. One that lets you go down to that level of detail if you know what you’re doing, and at the same time lets you create a simple agent that works well and efficiently without touching anything. We exposed the ceiling and forgot the floor: the platform was far too permeable to creating inefficient agents by default — thousands of tools and enormously heavy contexts loaded at the start of every session. The result was slow, imprecise, expensive agents, and users coming back with a phrase that stung: “it works for me in Claude Code.” Tool search and smart context loading improved things a lot, but the mistake was one of design: the right configuration should have been the default configuration.


The second is training and hands-on support — and not just any kind. As a platform team, our customer had always been technology people; with AgentOS our users were operations, business, finance, support. Explaining how to use the tool wasn’t enough: the leap that was hard for them was looking at their own work and seeing which part an agent could do. That’s not solved by documentation or a wizard — it’s solved by sitting down with each team, and we should have been there from day one. It’s the least scalable work there is, and it’s what was missing the most.


## What we learned


None of this is universal truth. It’s what worked for us, in our company, at this moment.


**Betting on protocols instead of providers gave us freedom of movement.** Eighteen months of leadership changes among providers, and we were never locked in.


**Build vs. buy changed its answer.** What used to be almost always buy is, in 2026, very often build — especially when what you want to build doesn’t exist on the market yet.


**Autonomy is built in layers.** Remote runtime, scheduled tasks, agent credentials, Slack identity. At least for us there was no shortcut: each layer unlocked the next, and we discovered each one by hitting the limits of the previous one.


**Don’t pay for what you’re not using.** Tool search, smart loading, and input/output files in the sandbox, on the context side; stateless runners and agents with no infrastructure of their own, on the infra side. All of them are the same idea: don’t load or sustain what isn’t needed.


**The most important: A platform doesn’t get adopted on its own.** You can have a thousand capabilities and it’s not enough: if you don’t flatten the learning curve and walk alongside the rest of the company as they learn and find their own use cases, what you built goes underused. It’s the least technical part of the job and the one that took us longest to see.


After eighteen months, the hardest part is no longer building capabilities. It’s understanding which ones to combine, and what for. Last month 245 new agents were created in AgentOS, and many of them do similar things: the same problem that led us to build AgentOS, now inside AgentOS. We’re starting to solve it with official agents and templates — the project manager, Talk2Data, the development agency — so that whoever needs one of those roles starts from something proven instead of from zero. We have a large set of ingredients and we’re still learning to cook with it.


That learning is not something we can do alone. That’s why today the bet is there: AI Champions across areas and roles, trainings for every level, an AgentOS Coach available on Slack, and a platform where creating an agent is a conversation, not a form.


And every new role will show us limits we can’t see today. That’s what has been happening since the beginning.
